name: owl

attributes.attribute: sign of age and wisdom to the Celts
Welsh flower-bride remade into an owl
appears in the epic of Kulhwch And Olwen without helping the hero
sister or twin of the man-eating Eghchte
read by some in the spiral art of old monuments

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: To the people of the Celtic lands, the owl carried a might spent on the night hunt. The bird stood for age and the knowing that age brings. The most cited owl in that canon is Blodeuwedd, a Welsh flower-bride remade into a bird after she cast aside her husband and urged a lover to kill him. The epic Kulhwch And Olwen names an owl of Cwm Cawlwyd, yet the bird cannot hand the hero the fact he lacks. Ireland keeps a faint owl goddess in Echtach, sister or twin of the man-eating Eghchte. Eye-shaped spirals etched on some early monuments of Ireland, Britain, and Wales lead a few writers to judge an owl-featured goddess. The claim pairs those stones with monuments that lie to the south and east across the Mediterranean.

okr.objective: Describe the owl as a Celtic symbol of age and wisdom.
key_results: To the Celts the owl carried age and the wisdom of age.
Blodeuwedd, a Welsh flower-bride, was remade into an owl.
Echtach stands as the sister or twin of the man-eating Eghchte.
Eye-shaped spirals on old monuments were read as the face of an owl goddess.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
